comment: Elements whose common aqueous redox couples exchange electrons fast enough (outer-sphere or low-barrier inner-sphere transfer, seconds to minutes at 10-100 mM) for the bench to see them. Couples of other elements (S, N, C, Cl, Co, ...) are kinetically inert on bench time unless their two forms differ by electrons only (oxygen-free forms with the same elements in whole-number multiples, X2 / X-: found by structure, `gem/redox.rs`), or they react through a registered kinetic row (measured rate law) or a species record that carries a self-exchange rate (RedoxCouple.k_self; the oxo-transfer couples of `data/redox_couples.json`). Thermodynamics decides *whether*, never *that* an inert couple reacts. Chromium is labile as a redox element: Cr(VI) is reduced by Fe(II), I-, sulfite, alcohols in seconds to minutes through Cr(V)/Cr(IV) (the substitution inertness of Cr(III) concerns its ligand exchange, not these electron transfers). Alkali / alkaline-earth metals (K, Li, Ca) and the aqua-ion metals Ni, Cd are labile: their couples have no electron-transfer barrier.
source: Taube, Chem. Rev. 50 (1952) 69 (labile vs inert complexes); Basolo & Pearson, Mechanisms of Inorganic Reactions; Marcus self-exchange tables (Sutin, Acc. Chem. Res. 1968) -- recalled, verify
fast_precipitating_comment: Compound solids that form from solution within seconds when their redox precursor is reduced or oxidised (amorphous hydrous oxides: manganese dioxide from permanganate). Every other compound solid that a discovered electron transfer could make in water (hematite, magnetite, cuprite, zincite, ...) has to nucleate and grow, which only the solubility table's precipitation model describes: they are not products of a discovered redox reaction unless they are already present. Elemental solids (cementation, plating) and registered minerals are always allowed.
